title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Beyond annotating your data, QualCoder provides powerful tools to analyze your results and make reports and graphs. If you want to report an issue in QualCoder or request an additional feature, please open a New issue on the GitHub repository for the project.
We’ll dive into five of the most frequently used tools, but bear in mind, there is much more to explore:
Other tools:

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Code retrieval
To have all the coded excerpts in one place to analyze your data as a whole, the best place to start is the Code retrieval (sometimes called the coding report) tool, which you can access in the top menu Analysis > Code retrieval.

Once you are there, the usual workflow is:

Choose one or more codes or categories.
Select one or more files. If you want to return all coded excerpts for the given code(s), select all the files.
Optionally narrow by case, attribute (e.g. only second-year students), or coder.
Click the Run button (as highlighted in red in the next screenshot) to show the results on the right pane.








TipTip: Selecting multiple files, codes or cases



Whenever you want to select multiple files, codes or cases, the fastest way is to use the Shift key. For example, if you want to select all the files, you would: 1) Select the first file, File 001, 2) Press and hold the Shift key, 3) Select the last file, File 010, 4) Release the Shift key.
To select multiple files one by one, press and hold the Ctrl or Cmd key while selecting the files.


You can analyze your data directly on this screen, scrolling up and down on the right pane. You can also export the results to HTML, TXT, CSV, XLSX, or ODT to read them in a different software.
Another option is use the matrix view, to place codes (or categories) against files or cases, so you can see who talked about what. This tool is located at the right of the Run button we used to show the results. You can export the resulting matrix to XLSX.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Code co-occurrence
This tool creates a matrix with all your codes both in the vertical and horizontal axes, each cell representing the number of times the given codes have overlapped or are right next to each other in your data. You can open it navigating to Analysis > Code co-occurrence.

Clicking on a cell shows the text where both codes have overlapped.

This is a useful result for your analysis, mainly in two ways:

If you notice redundant codes (being used for the same phenomenon), you could make the decision to merge the codes.
You spot a pattern where different codes tend to be close together in multiple cases, which you could infer as a relationship between two phenomena, an emerging theme.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Charts
There are a number of different graphs with aggregated data you can easily generate and export.
Going to Reports > Charts shows the available charts. For all of them you can filter what data is included in the plot with the options below “Data filters”.

Pie and sunburst and treemap charts, to show the relative frequency (percentage) of times a code is used.
Bar and cumulative bar charts, to show the absolute frequency (number) of times a code is used, per file or case if you choose a cumulative bar chart.
Heatmaps to show and compare visually the frequency a code is used by file or case.
Attribute charts to describe your cases or files by the attributes you have assigned them.
Word clouds to show the most frequent words in your coded data.







TipActivity: Explore the charts available



Choose one of the available charts and try it out. Then, write a little analysis about what the graph is showing.


Once the plot shows up in your web browser, you can download it by clicking the camera icon on the top-left corner.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
File and code summaries
In the Reports menu you can find File summary and Code summary.

File summary shows the following statistics for the file you select on the left pane:

Total number of characters, words, and unique words on the file
Top 100 words in the file and their frequency. Make sure to filter out common words (also known as stopwords), with the drop-down menu shown in the screenshot below
For each code used in the file: the number of times it was used, the number of characters that the coded text contains, and a percentage calculated on the total number of characters in the document



- On the other hand, Code summary shows: - Coders and files that used the code - Number of times the code has been used, along with the number of characters in the excerpts and the average per excerpt - Number of words and unique words on the coded excerpts - Top 100 words on the excerpts and their frequency. The option to remove stopwords is also available here

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Database queries
QualCoder gives us the great feature to directly access the database behind all our data, accessible in Reports > Database queries. For users who are comfortable with SQL queries, it will be useful to get custom reports from their project.
Let’s see three examples:

Using a default query to list files not including a given code

On the left pane, scroll all the way down to “Default Queries”
Select “FILES THAT ARE NOT CODED with code id 1”
Click the Run button to execute the query
The result shows the files that don’t have the code with ID 1, which in our example represents “bestpractice”

You can see the query includes not only coded text (code_text), but also audio/video (code_av) and images (code_image)
Try modifying the query to use a different code ID, or to show the files that do have the code





Let’s write ourselves a simple query, returning all file names where the full text contains the word “github”
SELECT id, name
FROM source
WHERE fulltext LIKE '%rstudio%' OR fulltext LIKE '%r studio%'
We could read this query as follows:

The database has a table of data called source, which contains all our file sources
This table has fields id, name, and fulltext, containing our files id, name and its entire text
We filter our results with the WHERE clause, filtering text that contains either “rstudio” or “r studio”

A more complex query, involving the code_name and code_text tables, searching for coded text that contains the word “jupyter”
SELECT source.name, code_name.name, code_text.seltext
FROM code_text
   JOIN source ON code_text.fid = source.id
   JOIN code_name ON code_text.cid = code_name.cid
WHERE code_text.seltext LIKE '%jupyter%'

If you want to learn more about databases and SQL, we invite you to read the Software Carpentry or Library Carpentry lessons.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Other tools

Code comparison and code frequencies
If your project involves multiple coders reviewing the same data, probably you will be interested in comparing their coding agreement. In other words, you’re interested in intercoder reliability, also known as inter-rater reliability. The tool in Reports > Comparison compares two coders on the same text using percentage agreement and Cohen’s kappa, a measure of agreement beyond chance.
Another tool to see the number of passages coded, disaggregated by code name and coder is found in Reports > Code frequencies
If you want are interested in learning more about intercoder reliability for your project, reach out to the Library’s Research Data Services department at rds@library.ucsb.edu.


Journals
Journals are free-form notes for recording ideas, decisions and emerging themes as you code. They support reflexivity: being aware of how your own views shape the analysis.

The journal window floats, so you can keep it open beside the coding screen.
Add simple formatting with Markdown: # for headings (up to three levels), *italics* and **bold**. Web links become clickable from the right-click menu.
Search journals, sort them by name or date, filter them, add attributes, and export one journal or all of them as a single file.

You can see and manage all your journals under Manage > Journals.






Note



Memo vs journal: a memo belongs to one code, file or passage; a journal entry is about the project as a whole.

title: Working in a Team
text:
QualCoder is single-user, so teams use one of two approaches. Either way, give every person a unique coder name (Project > Settings > Change).








Approach
How it works
Best for




Take turns
One person works, closes QualCoder, then passes the zipped project to the next person. Never open the same project at the same time.
Small groups, open (inductive) coding


Master project + merge
Build one master project with all files, give each person a copy, code separately, then merge the copies back. Don’t edit the texts in the copies.

text:
Merging Projects
Open the destination project, then use Help > Special functions > Merge projects, choose the source project and run the merge.






Important



Back up the destination project first. Important: There is no undo!



Files, codes and categories that don’t already exist are added.
Coding of text, images and audio/video, plus cases, attributes and journals, is brought across.
Existing attribute values in the destination are not overwritten.
If two people edited the same text file differently, codes may land in the wrong place.

title: Introduction to Qualitative Data Analysis
text:
Qualitative data, such as interview transcripts, open-ended survey answers, field notes, focus group recordings, videos and news articles, is rich but unruly:

No fixed structure: Responses wander, contradict themselves or bury the main point.
Inconsistent format: It spans text, audio and video, and answers range from one word to several paragraphs.
Harder to compare and count: The same idea shows up in different words, so it has to be interpreted rather than tallied.
Volume: A few hours of audio recordings or video can fill hundreds of pages.
Ambiguity: Tone and context carry meaning that’s easy to misread.

Despite these challenges, qualitative data is sometimes the most appropriate, or even the only, way to understand a research phenomenon, depending on what that phenomenon is. For example, a survey can show how many employees are leaving a company, but only interviews can reveal why they decided to go.
Qualitative data analysis is about finding patterns, unfolding both explicit and implicit attitudes, behaviors, and beliefs, understanding meanings and events, and making sense of findings concerning the research questions at hand.
But how do we move from text to meaningful findings? This is where coding comes in. Coding is the process of assigning labels to meaningful parts of our data so we can identify patterns, compare experiences, and develop interpretations. Importantly, coding is not simply highlighting interesting quotes. The way we code influences what we notice, how we interpret people’s experiences, and ultimately the conclusions we draw.
A single hour-long interview can run to a couple of pages, and a small-scale study can produce hundreds. Coding is how we turn that volume into something we can think with: we read closely, attach short labels to meaningful segments, and then group, compare and count those labels across the whole dataset. Without coding, analysis tends to rely on whichever quotes felt most vivid; with it, we can see which ideas recur, which are rare, and which participants hold them.
This process involves identifying and labeling meaningful pieces of qualitative data. These labels, called codes, help organize the data and make it easier to identify important ideas, concepts, and patterns. Coding is an initial step in qualitative data analysis that supports a closer examination of the data and provides a foundation for further analysis and interpretation.






NoteActivity 0.1 - Warm-up



Imagine you’re a researcher studying how new developers experience Git. You’ve just finished an interview, and this is one passage from the transcript. Your job is to read between the lines: what is this person going through, and what’s worth capturing?

Interviewer: Can you tell me about a memorable experience you’ve had using Git?
Participant: Sure. In my first internship I merged my feature branch into main and got fourteen conflicts. I kept staring at the angle brackets and equals signs, reading the same lines over and over, and I still couldn’t tell which half was mine and which was my teammate’s. I didn’t even understand why some files had conflicts when I was sure I’d never touched them. So I started googling, and pretty soon I had about twenty tabs open, rebase, reset, revert, cherry-pick, and they all started blurring together. Every answer I found brought up three new terms I’d have to look up, and at some point I was just scrolling without taking anything in. I remember sitting there with the terminal open, not even sure what I was supposed to type next.

Discuss with a partner or share in the chat

What labels did you both come up with?
The participant never says how they feel. So how did you know?






Data can be arranged and coded following two types of approaches: a more inductive (bottom-up) approach, where insights and themes emerge more organically and directly from the data without prior assumptions, or a deductive (top-down) approach, where researchers apply preexisting theoretical frameworks or concepts to the data. The approaches can also be combined as researchers engage with and learn more details from the data.

The bottom-up approach is exploratory and highly flexible as there are no predetermined categories or hypotheses; it has its basis in grounded theory, meaning that themes emerge directly from the data through open coding and analysis, allowing a wide range of topics and potential unexpected insights to be extracted from the data.
In contrast, the top-down approach starts with an existing theoretical framework or research question. Researchers go into the data with predefined hypotheses, and the analysis focuses on confirming or refuting them. This gives the research process clear direction. However, it can also limit the analysis, because perspectives or themes that the original framework didn’t anticipate may be overlooked.
To see the difference, go back to our Git example. Earlier, you made up your own labels as you read and let the terms vary as much as the data suggested. With a top-down approach, you would instead start from a predefined list of codes, such as confusion and overload, drawn from previous research or an established framework. Your task would be to find where each code appears in the transcript, rather than creating new ones.
It’s important to remember that, although it’s helpful to understand the differences between these two approaches, they can actually work well together. Combining them allows you to take advantage of each method’s strengths, leading to a richer and more nuanced analysis that incorporates real-world data and theoretical insights.



Coding also makes our reasoning visible and accountable, and this is where tools matter. On paper, coding three sentences is manageable; coding 300 pages is not. Renaming a code, finding every passage tagged “trust,” comparing two coders, or checking which participants raised an idea all mean flipping through stacks of highlighted pages. Qualitative Data Analysis Software (QDAS) does not do the thinking for us, but it handles the bookkeeping: it stores the codebook, retrieves every coded segment in seconds, merges and renames codes everywhere at once, and links each finding back to its source. That frees our attention for the interpretive work that only a researcher can do.
But why do we need a software? Conducting qualitative data analysis manually or without dedicated tools can quickly become overwhelming. Imagine tracking hundreds of sticky notes, comments, and highlighted passages across dozens of participant documents. As the volume of data grows, it becomes increasingly difficult to keep each insight connected to its original source, remember who said what, compare responses across participants, and identify patterns consistently. Important details can be overlooked, connections can be lost, and verifying interpretations becomes time-consuming. QDAS helps manage this complexity by keeping data organized, searchable, and traceable to its source, allowing researchers to spend less time managing information and more time interpreting meaning.




The dataset and documentation for this workshop is adapted from a real research project that is publicly archived in the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR):

Rampin, Vicky; Nguyễn, Sarah. 2020. “Investigating and Archiving the Scholarly Git Experience.” Qualitative Data Repository. https://doi.org/10.5064/F6VOIB8H. V2.

The original project, funded by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, is a mixed-methods study of how scholars use Git and Git hosting platforms. It draws on focus groups, a survey and interviews. To make the data easier to work with in a short session, we have simplified, trimmed and restructured parts of it.
Please note: the adapted version is for teaching only and should not be used for research or cited as a source. The original dataset and its documentation in QDR are the official record. If you want to use this data in your own work, please download it directly from QDR and cite the original authors.

title: Meet QualCoder!
text:
QualCoder is a free, open-source desktop program for qualitative data analysis. It helps you organize non-numeric data, such as interviews, documents and images, and tag meaningful passages with codes.
QualCoder began with a researcher’s own frustration. While analyzing survey data for his PhD, he relied on a free coding tool that had become hard to install and keep running, so he rebuilt the workflow from scratch in Python and shared the result with everyone. That spirit still drives the project: qualitative analysis shouldn’t depend on expensive licenses or institutional subscriptions.
QualCoder is maintained by a small team of academics working across four continents, often in their own time. Despite these constraints, the team has continued to improve the software, responding to user feedback and incorporating suggestions to make it more useful and accessible to a growing global community.
What you can do with it:

Code many kinds of data: text, PDFs, images, audio and video.
Write as you think: keep journals and attach memos to codes, files and coded passages.
Organize ideas: group codes into categories in a tree, like folders.
Analyze and report: retrieve everything tagged with a code, compare codes, and export reports.
Use optional AI tools: search for themes and discuss your data with a large language model. These are switched off by default.

Applications
QualCoder can be used to analyze a wide range of qualitative data files and combine them within the same research project. For example, students can import PDF files such as journal articles, policy documents, reports, or case studies and code them to identify key themes and concepts; audio recordings of interviews or focus groups can be transcribed and coded to explore participants’ experiences, opinions, and perceptions; text files such as open-ended survey responses, interview transcripts, field notes, or meeting notes can be organized into categories and themes; web-based or social-media text can be analyzed to compare public perspectives and discussions; and images or other visual materials such as photographs, screenshots, or field observations can be coded alongside textual data. These different file types can also be combined and compared, allowing students to examine, for example, whether themes identified in policy documents are also reflected in interviews, survey responses, or public discussions.






NoteRound-Robin



How do you envision using QualCoder in your research or coursework? What types of documents or artifacts would you analyze (e.g., journal articles, policy documents, interview recordings, transcripts, survey responses, or images)?


Good to know:

It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and works offline.
It is designed for one person at a time. Teams take turns on a project or merge copies later (see Working in a team).
It aims to follow the REFI-QDA exchange standard, so projects can move to and from tools such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA, with some limits.
It is licensed under the LGPL v3. If you use it in coursework or research, cite it (the citation is on the QualCoder website).

The simplest route to install the software is to follow the instructions on the setup page . For updated instructions from QualCoder themselves, download the ready-made installer from the releases page. Choose the one appropriate for your laptop.








System
What to download
What to expect on first launch




Windows
The Windows installer (.exe)
A SmartScreen warning, because the app is not signed. Click More info, then Run anyway.


macOS
The .dmg file
A Gatekeeper warning. Allow the app under System Settings > Privacy & Security.


Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
The Linux executable, or run from source
Usually no warning.

VLC media player is needed to code audio and video
ffmpeg lets QualCoder draw audio waveforms.

These different file types can also be combined and compared, allowing students to examine, for example, whether themes identified in policy documents are also reflected in interviews, survey responses, or public discussions.

text:
Basic Preferences/Settings
We’ll start by adjusting a few settings. Open the main menu and choose QualCoder > Preferences (Mac) or Project > Settings (Windows).

Only a few settings matter for now:

Coder name: Every code you apply is stamped with your coder name. Set your own name (or initials) before you start, using the Change button. This matters later if you compare coding with a collaborator. For this, choose change and rename the system default.

Show IDs: It is a good practice to check this option so that you will see the unique ID for each file, code, cases and other project components.
Language: English is the default. French, German and Spanish are kept up to date; other languages are contributed by volunteers.
Font and display: Increase the font size if text is hard to read on a projector or small screen.
Backups: QualCoder can back up your project every hour and keep the most recent copies, named like projectname_BKP_yyyymmdd_hh.qda. Let’s leave this on!

Applying these changes, your settings and preferences should look like:

As you may notice, QualCoder offers several additional settings, including options for integrating AI into your project. Don’t worry about these for now—we’ll explore them later in the workshop.






NoteActivity 1.1 – Adding Yourself as a Coder



Enter your name or initials so QualCoder can identify who is coding the data. Then, add a second coder (you may add any name), but keep you as the current coder. We will see how that works in practice in future episodes.








TipPro-tip: Resetting preferences or coders from past projects



If you already use QualCoder and want to start from a blank slate, you can clear the settings, recent projects and saved coder name left over from earlier work. Your existing projects won’t be affected. QualCoder keeps these preferences in a hidden folder called .qualcoder in your home directory. Your projects are stored separately as .qda folders, so resetting preferences doesn’t touch them.
To reset your preferences:

Quit QualCoder
Rename the preferences folder

macOS / Linux (Terminal): mv ~/.qualcoder ~/.qualcoder_backup
Windows (PowerShell): Rename-Item "$HOME\.qualcoder" ".qualcoder_backup"

Reopen QualCoder. It will start fresh, with no recent projects and no saved coder name.

Tip: Renaming the folder instead of deleting it keeps a backup. To undo the reset, rename .qualcoder_backup back to .qualcoder. Coder names are saved inside each project’s .qda file, so a new project starts with no coders from earlier projects.

title: Coding Data
text:
As discussed earlier, coding involves assigning a short label or tag (hereafter mostly referred to as a code) to a passage of data that expresses an idea relevant to your research question. Codes are then grouped into categories, which may eventually develop into broader themes, which usually will determine your analysis report structure.
For research on learning version control, such as Git, codes capture specific ideas in participants’ responses, categories group related codes and their sub-codes, and themes express broader patterns across the data.

Codes are the foundation for every level above them, so it’s worth deciding early how you’ll create them. As covered earlier, codes can be planned in advance from theory (deductive), emerge as you read the data (inductive), or come from a mix of both. In this workshop, we’ll start with a predefined codebook.

title: Coding Data
text:
Codebook
As we start assigning codes to excerpts we start developing what it is called a codebook. In qualitative research, a codebook is the shared framework that turns raw text into analyzable data. Each entry typically names a code, gives a concise definition (memo), and sets inclusion and exclusion criteria for when the code applies and when it doesn’t.
Similarly to codes, codebooks can be built deductively from theory or prior literature, inductively from patterns that emerge during close reading, or through a mix of both. Often it changes over several rounds as the team refines, merges, splits, or retires codes. That evolution is itself part of the analytic record, so keeping versions and logging changes helps document how interpretations developed.
When several researchers code the same material, the codebook keeps them aligned. It makes inter-coder agreement possible to assess, and it gives the team a concrete reference for talking through disagreements instead of relying on each person’s intuition.
Beyond the life of a single project, a well-documented codebook makes qualitative work more transparent and credible. Readers and reviewers can see how claims were grounded in the data, and other researchers can understand, critique, or adapt the analytic approach. It also makes archived qualitative data far more usable for secondary analysis, since the meaning behind each code stays clear long after the original team has moved on.

title: Coding Data
text:
Importing a Codebook
To get started, we’ve prepared a sample codebook. Starting from a set of predefined codes is typical of a deductive approach. Later, we’ll also try an inductive approach, where we create new codes for themes that come up as we read the transcripts.
You can export a codebook from QualCoder and share it as a .qdc file (Qualitative Data Codebook). If you’re starting a project from scratch, as we did, and using a deductive approach, you can also import a list of codes from a plain-text file. Each code can include a description (memo) to clarify its meaning and intended use. Alternatively, you can create codes manually, one at a time. However, given our limited time, we’ll use the import option to get started more efficiently.
In the project example folder,locate the file Steeves_Interview_Codebook.csv and open it in a text editor or spreadsheet program.

The first column contains the code names, and the second contains each code’s description, which QualCoder imports as the code’s memo. Notice the double angle brackets (>>) in some code names. They show how a code that relates to a higher-level category. For example, emotion>>confused means the code confused belongs under the category emotion.






NoteActivity 3.1 - Import the codebook in csv format



Alright, let’s now import the codebook by following Project > Import > Import plain text codes list.



Great! You should now see your list of codes in the lower-right panel. Each code has been given a color automatically. You can change these colors under Code > Color Scheme. Colors give you quick visual cues, and giving related codes similar shades makes them easier to spot together. For now, we’ll leave the default colors as they are.

To add a level to the codebook hierarchy, right-click a category or code and create a subcategory or subcode beneath it or rearrange its structure using by navigating options in Modify.

Clicking Memo opens a separate window with the code’s description. Expect to revise these descriptions as your analysis develops. As you code more transcripts, you’ll find edge cases and clarify where one code ends and another begins.

title: Coding Data
text:
Building & Organizing the Code Tree
Codebooks are represented hierarchically as a tree: categories act like folders, codes sit inside them, and can also have subcodes. A code can belong to only one category. If an idea fits in two places, we recommend creating two similarly named codes.
While we will stick to this structure for this workshop, you can rearrange things, through right-clicking for options to move, merge, delete, sort and more.
For a bigger clean-up, open the Code Organizer under Coding. It shows your codes and categories as a diagram you can restructure: move, merge, rename and remove codes and categories, add new categories, and export the view as a PNG.
With files and our code tree in place, let’s get started with practicing some coding.

title: Coding Data
text:
Coding text step by step
Open Coding > Code text. The code tree sits on the left, your document in the center, and the file list nearby.
We will start by examining File 02. Since we won’t have time to examine the entire file, let’s scroll down to line 120. Great! We can now see the excerpt where the interviewer asks, “VS: So can you just narrate what you’re doing there?”
Although we don’t need to read every detail, we can see that the interviewee is describing a process while expressing uncertainty, frustration, and confusion.
Select the paragraph at line 122. Our codebook already includes the code confused under the category emotion (Emotion > Confused), so we can apply it to this excerpt by clicking the code.
Note that the selected passage takes on the code’s color, and a number appears next to the code showing how many times it has been applied. That count also adds to the total for its parent category, Emotion. The parent’s number is the total for all of its sub-codes. This lets you see how often a broad concept or idea comes up, as well as each specific variation of it.

If you select a text segment by mistake or need to undo the coding, you can right-click the selection and select Unmark (U). Shortcuts after highlighting: Q reuses your most recent code, R lists recent codes, and V makes an in vivo code from the selected words.

Let’s move to File 07. Before we start, look at the code list. The number next to confused is gone, but emotion still shows 1. The code list only shows counts for the file that’s currently open, so confused has no count in file 07. Emotion still shows 1 because the code you applied in the previous file still counts toward it. In a later episode, we’ll explore reports that summarize code counts across all your files.
Don’t worry, your previous work is safe! Yhe coding you completed in the previous file has been saved. As we discussed earlier, QualCoder is set to back up your work automatically according to your preferences.
Going back to File 07, let’s look for line 71, where the interviewee starts describing their approach to editing multiple files in the repository. Skim through the passage, for this exercise we will consider it expresses confidence in the workflow, and code it as determined.

title: Coding Data
text:
Uncoding Things
Coding mistakes are inevitable, so part of good practice is going back to remove codes that don’t fit.






NoneActivity 3.2 - Practicing Uncoding



MK – File 00004 | Lines 125–132

SN: What would you, where would you go to find these types of recent these better resources?

MK: Probably the carpentries? That’s maybe a little biased because I’ve taught and helped with teaching for their Git lessons but I know what’s in them and I know it works. So that’s where I would go.

Code this excerpt with any term that represents what you took from reading it.
Next, let’s uncode it, assuming you want to check with your team the criteria for adding new codes to the predefined codebook.








ImportantDiscussion point: Should you code the interviewer’s question?





Usually no. Code only the participant’s words. Including the interviewer’s questions can:

inflate your counts, and
credit participants with ideas the interviewer introduced.

This matters even more when interviewers ask different follow-ups, because the questions won’t line up across interviews.
The exception: Include the question when the answer doesn’t make sense without it.

SN: Would you teach someone the same way?
MK: Absolutely not.

On its own, “Absolutely not” means nothing.
A simple test: If someone reads this segment alone, will they understand it?
Important: Always write the rule in your project documentation and apply it every time.




Coding with Search Assistance
See the question mark on the left-hand side of the top bar? That allows us to search for words across files, and can be useful to identify relevant terms before we apply codes.
Let’s look for GUI, which stands for Graphic User Interface, and apply the GUI code the excerpts with the first 5 results (in order of appearance). Select “Aa” to make the search case sensitive, and navigate matches across files using the arrows.


Where should a selection begin and end?
Deciding how much text to select is one of the main choices you make when coding. A few guidelines:

Select a complete thought: Start where the participant begins the idea and stop when they finish it or move on to a new topic. That might be a phrase, a sentence or a whole paragraph.
Include enough context to understand it later: Someone reading the excerpt by itself, for example in a report, should still be able to tell why it was coded. If “It was a nightmare” only makes sense with the sentence before it, select both sentences.
Leave out what doesn’t belong: Don’t add filler, the interviewer’s next question or a new topic just to fill out the excerpt. Extra text makes reports harder to read and blurs what the code means.
Overlapping is fine: A passage can have more than one code, and selections for different codes can overlap. For example, one sentence might be coded Confused while the whole paragraph is coded GUI.
Be consistent. Use the same approach across all transcripts, especially if you’re coding with other people. Some teams agree on a default unit, such as “the full answer to one question,” before they start.

title: Coding Data
text:
In Vivo Coding
As most QDAS, QualCoder also offers the option for researchers to apply InVivo coding. In vivo coding means using the participant’s own words as the name of a code. Instead of making up a label such as Frustration, you take a short phrase straight from the transcript, such as “I just nuked the whole repo.” In vivo is Latin for “in the living,” meaning the code comes from the data itself.
In vivo coding is an inductive approach because the codes come from the transcripts, not from a predefined codebook. It’s useful when you want to:

keep participants’ voices and terms in your analysis
capture slang, jargon or vivid expressions that a generic label would lose
start exploring data before you have a clear set of themes

In vivo codes are often renamed or grouped into broader categories later. For example, “I just nuked the whole repo” might end up under the existing code conflict-burn-repo. Let’s select File 04 and look for line 131, where the interviewer mentions The Carpentries, and let’s apply an in vivo code to that, using the right-click or the shortcut (Command or Ctrl + V).
The rationale here would be to add it as in vivo for now, until they consult with the PI and review strategies.






NoteActivity 3.3 - In Vivo Coding Discussion



At what point do in vivo codes need to become conceptual? Does grouping or renaming them erase the participant’s voice? Where should that decision be recorded?



Add your Reasoning
Codes show what you noticed. Memos and annotations record why. Memos are notes recording the researcher’s thoughts, interpretations, questions, or decisions during analysis.
Writing down your reasoning as you go makes your analysis easier to explain, review and share with others.
These notes become a record of how your thinking developed. They’re especially useful when you refine codes, merge or split them, or code with other people.






NoteActivity 3.4 - Adding a Memo to a Code



Based on what you know about The Carpentries, add a one sentence memo to it, also noting it is derived from In Vivo Coding.

title: Coding Data
text:
Auto-coding (use with care!)
Auto-code in QualCoder applies a code to every passage that matches text you specify, so you don’t have to select each passage by hand. You’ll find the options as buttons at the top right of the text-coding window. First select the code you want to apply, then choose an option:

Auto-code exact text codes every occurrence of a word or phrase. QualCoder asks which files to search, so you can code across several transcripts at once. Separate alternatives with | to catch several terms with one code, for example GitHub Desktop|GUI. Matching is case-sensitive.
Auto-code sentences codes the whole sentence that contains a text fragment, not just the fragment. You can set what counts as the end of a sentence. The default is a period followed by a space.
Auto-code between start and end marks codes everything between a start text and an end text in the current file. It’s useful for structured transcripts, such as coding everything from one interview question to the next.
Regex is a checkbox that lets you use regular expressions for more flexible matching, such as wildcards and word variations.
First or last match only is a right-click option that codes only the first or last match in each file.
Mark speakers codes each paragraph with the speaker’s name when transcripts label speakers as [name], {name} or name:.
Undo reverses recent auto-coding, but only until you close the project.

For the workshop, keep in mind that auto-coding matches words, not meaning. Searching for “confused” won’t catch “I had no idea what was going on,” and it will catch “I wasn’t confused at all.” Treat auto-coding as a first pass, and review every coded passage before you rely on it.
Buttons at the top right can code every exact match of a word (case-sensitive; separate options with |, e.g. exam|exams), every sentence containing a fragment, or the section between two markers.






WarningReversing Auto-Coding in QualCoder



In QualCoder, auto-coding actions can only be undone while the project remains open. Once you close the project, the option to reverse these actions may no longer be available. Therefore, it is important to carefully review the results of auto-coding before closing the project. Check that the assigned codes are relevant to the selected text, accurately reflect the intended meaning, and are consistent with your coding framework. If any errors or inappropriate code assignments are identified, correct them before closing the project. Proceed with caution, as auto-coding may produce results that require manual verification to ensure the accuracy and reliability of your qualitative data analysis.

title: AI Features
text:
Available tools
QualCoder offers AI features designed to support, rather than replace, your qualitative analysis. The AI assists by suggesting, searching, and synthesizing patterns, while the researcher retains full control over interpretation and decision-making.

The AI Agent
The AI Agent is a dedicated chat interface accessible in its own tab or dockable as a sidebar. It analyzes your coding system, memos, coded passages, cases, and attributes, enabling semantic, keyword, and regular expression searches across your corpus.
The agent prompts for confirmation before applying major changes, marks all created items as “AI Agent,” and allows you to revert recent actions. It cannot modify your original source documents.
You can start a conversation in four ways:

New, open chat: The most flexible option for exploring emerging ideas, identifying comparable cases, evaluating overlapping codes, or retrieving information across documents.
Topic exploration: Describe a topic, choose documents or cases, and pick an analytic prompt (topic-summary, analyze-differences, or analyze-unexpected).
Text analysis: Highlight a passage in the text coding workspace and right-click to open AI Text Analysis. Use it for close reading, brainstorming interpretations, or discussing ambiguities. Results can be saved as an annotation.
Code analysis: Analyze data aggregated under specific codes or categories. Useful workflows include:

Summarizing all content associated with a given code
Comparing overlapping codes to clarify category boundaries
Critiquing code definitions in light of the underlying data
Evaluating theoretical saturation by searching for uncoded variations, borderline cases, and counterexamples








Tip



Additional tools available from the AI menu:

Prompt Library: Save and reuse your own prompts and analytic strategies. Call them in chat with slash notation (e.g. /in-vivo-coding). Saved prompts also appear within topic, text, and code analysis menus.
Check project AI readiness: Reviews project setup and provides recommendations to optimize AI performance.
Ask the AI agent (Help menu): Answers questions about using QualCoder, based on its documentation.





AI-assisted coding
FIXME: Change coders
This demonstration illustrates how to identify candidate excerpts matching a specific code using QualCoder’s AI capabilities. This feature is accessible via Coding > AI-assisted coding, AI > AI-assisted coding, or the “AI Assistance” tab within the text coding workspace (Coding > Code text).
This process provides assisted rather than automated coding. QualCoder presents recommended excerpts alongside the model’s rationale, leaving final coding decisions to you (unlike the automated, keyword-based auto-code tool).
To start, select a code (or enter a topic), select an analytic prompt, and optionally filter by document, case, or attribute. QualCoder searches its local memory before querying the language model to rank and explain match results.
In the text coding workspace, click <Start AI Search>, as shown below:
{fig-alt=“Screenshot of the Text Coding Workspace, with the”Start AI Search” button highligted in red”}
Next, specify: 1) The target code to search for 2) Optional data filters (file, case, or attribute) 3) The desired analytic prompt
QualCoder includes three default analytic (system) prompts, which you can modify or create new ones:

Content analysis with coding rules: Instructs the AI to follow coding rules outlined in the code memo.
Focused search: Best suited for well-defined topics; returns fewer, highly precise results.
Open search: Identifies a broader range of potentially relevant material, which may yield more unrelated results.

QualCoder will start looking for relevant passages and send them to the AI to decide if they are indeed appropriate for the code or not. Results populate in the left panel. Selecting an item allows you to review the passage and confirm the code assignment. A prompt will ask whether you wish to attach the AI’s explanation as a memo.

title: Setting Up Your Project
text:
On the main window, before exploring QualCoder and its features, let’s create a new project. For this workshop, let’s save the project in a folder called “Workshop” your Desktop so it’s easy to locate and access. Choose Project > Create New Project.

Next, let’s name the project git-experience. Note that this will create a folder named git-experience.qda inside your selected folder. Open it, and you’ll see a set of predefined subfolders:

This is a QualCoder project folder. QualCoder saves each project as an ordinary folder whose name ends in .qda. Here’s what each item in it does:

git-experience.qda/ is the project itself. To open it, choose Project → Open in QualCoder and select this folder. If you move or back up the project, copy the whole folder. Taking only some of the files inside will break it.
data.qda is the most important file. It’s a SQLite database that holds all your analysis work: Your codes and code categories (the code tree). Every coded segment of text, image, audio and video. Cases, attributes, journals and memos. The plain text QualCoder pulls out of your imported documents (this is the text you actually code). Project settings and the list of imported files
project_in_use.lock is a temporary file. QualCoder creates it when the project is open, so the same project can’t be edited from two places at once.
ai_data/ holds data for QualCoder’s AI-assisted features. It’s a local vector database of embeddings made from your documents, which powers AI search and AI-assisted coding. QualCoder can rebuild it from your documents.
documents/ stores copies of the text files you imported (.txt, .docx, .pdf, .odt and so on). Your coding is tied to the extracted text in data.qda, not to these files.
images/ stores imported images (.jpg, .png and so on) that you can code by region.
audio/ stores imported audio (.mp3, .wav, .m4a and so on). You can transcribe it and code it by time segment.
video/ stores imported video (.mp4, .mov and so on), which you can also transcribe and code by time segment.

text:
Navigating Basic Functions
The main screen has five tabs: Project, Manage, Coding, Reports, AI and Help. But since our project is empty there isn’t much to explore yet.

Adding a Project Memo
The first step will be to add a project memo. Adding a short memo (about 300–700 characters) describing your research question and data is good practice for future reference and clarity about the project goals and methodology.

Let’s copy the content from the project-memo.rtf file located in the documentation subfolder of the workshop folder and paste it:

Project Memo: Investigating & Archiving the Scholarly Git Experience (IASGE) - Behavioral Study
This project contains the data underlying the behavioral study of Investigating & Archiving the Scholarly Git Experience (IASGE). The study investigates how scholars use Git and Git hosting platforms (GHPs), such as GitHub and GitLab, to conduct research, manage scholarly materials, and collaborate with others. It explores how researchers with varying levels of experience adopt version control in their workflows, what challenges they encounter, how they learn to use these tools, and how libraries and other scholarly support organizations can better support the sustainable management and preservation of research outputs.
Research Questions and Objectives
The study seeks to understand how scholars incorporate Git and Git hosting platforms into individual and collaborative research practices. It considers both scholars who actively use Git in their academic work and those who are familiar with Git but have not fully adopted it into a standardized workflow. The research examines how these groups use platform features, learn version control practices, and navigate the technical and social aspects of collaborative research.
Key research questions include:

How do scholars with different levels of experience use Git and Git hosting platforms in their research workflows?
How do researchers learn Git, find instructions, and develop practices for managing files, tracking changes, and synchronizing collaborative work?
How do scholars resolve merge conflicts, reuse and adapt existing code, and communicate with collaborators or external researchers through issues, discussions, and other platform features?
How do researchers discover, evaluate, reuse, and cite code hosted in public repositories?
What challenges do scholars encounter when using Git hosting platforms for academic collaboration, and what features or improvements would better support their needs?
How can libraries and other scholarly support services help researchers make their code, data, and other research outputs citable, stable, accessible, and suitable for long-term preservation?

Research Design and Methods
The behavioral study uses a three-part, mixed-methods empirical approach consisting of focus groups, a survey, and semi-structured interviews. These methods provide complementary perspectives on scholarly users’ experiences, practices, preferences, and needs.
Focus groups gather perspectives on Git adoption, research collaboration, common challenges, and opportunities for improving scholarly workflows. The survey collects information about users’ backgrounds, experience levels, platform use, feature adoption, and research practices. Semi-structured interviews provide a more detailed examination of individual experiences through open-ended questions and task-based scenarios. Together, these methods support an understanding of both broader usage patterns and the reasoning behind specific user behaviors.
During interviews, participants discuss their research processes and demonstrate how they approach representative Git and Git hosting platform tasks. Scenarios include editing multiple files, comparing versions of a document, synchronizing local and remote repositories, resolving conflicts, forking repositories, and collaborating with other researchers. Additional tasks explore how participants communicate feedback about code, submit or respond to issues, search for reusable code, obtain citations for repositories, and arrange for persistent identifiers and long-term preservation of research materials. Participants are also asked how they learned each task, where they seek instructions, and how they would teach the same practices to others.
Data and Scope
The project data include, but are not limited to, information about participant experiences and practices, user profiles, levels of Git experience, frequency of feature use, collaboration patterns, learning strategies, and perceptions of platform functionality. Data generated through the study’s research methods provide insight into how scholars engage with version control and Git hosting platforms across different stages of adoption.
The interview component also captures participants’ approaches to specific tasks, their decision-making processes, the resources they consult, and the difficulties they encounter. These observations help distinguish between knowing that a feature exists and being able to use it effectively in a research context. The study further considers participants’ preferences for collaboration, peer feedback, code reuse, citation, and repository preservation.
Significance and Expected Outcomes
The findings aim to inform how libraries, research support professionals, and platform developers can better meet the needs of scholars using Git and Git hosting platforms. By identifying common practices, barriers to adoption, and gaps in existing learning resources, the study can help shape instruction, training, and support services for researchers at different experience levels.
Ultimately, the behavioral study contributes to IASGE’s broader goal of understanding how scholarly materials hosted on Git platforms can transition from active, collaborative development to stable, permanently citable research outputs supported by professional preservation practices. The project provides an empirical basis for improving the discoverability, usability, citation, and long-term accessibility of scholarship created and shared through Git-based research workflows.


Project memos can also provide context for AI tools integrated into QualCoder, helping them generate more relevant, consistent, and contextually informed suggestions and analyses. Any text written after a line containing ##### remains private and is not shared with the AI model. In the example below, however, we will keep the entire memo visible to the AI to demonstrate how project-level context can inform its responses later in the workshop.

title: Setting Up Your Project
text:
Managing/Importing Files
With the project memo in place, let’s bring in the data we’ll be working with by importing the interview files we’ll code and analyze.
All data in QualCoder comes in through Manage > Manage Files.







Type
Accepted Formats




Text
.txt, .docx, .epub, .md, .odt, .pdf, .rtf, .tex


Images
.jpg, .jpeg, .png


Audio and video
.mp3, .m4a, .wav, .mp4, .mov, .ogg (and .wmv video)



Click the first icon (the document with a plus sign) to import files. A window should open, allowing you to browse for and select the files you downloaded for this workshop. We will be uploading 10 interview transcripts that use aliases instead of participants’ real names to protect their identities.



The files should be displayed in our window, and double-clicking a file should open and display its contents.







ImportantPrepare Data Before Importing into QualCoder



QualCoder should not be used to edit, de-identify, or pseudonymize raw data. Although pseudonymization is a newly released feature, it is not yet sufficiently robust for routine use. Best practice is to import only finalized, analysis-ready transcripts and notes into the platform for coding.


The memo field can be used to record any notes or annotations relevant to the file, including its relationship to other files or data sources.
More generally, the memo can capture contextual information, methodological notes, or other details that help document the file and support subsequent analysis. We won’t be using file memos in this workshop, but you may find them useful in your own projects for documenting additional information about your data and keeping track of details that may be relevant during analysis.
Note that that the time and date stamp reflect the import, not the file creation. IDs are sequentially assigned and depends on how you have selected the imported files. But what are cases for?

Cases
Cases allow you to group data around a person, place, organization, or situation. In QualCoder, a case provides a way to bring together files and descriptive information associated with the same entity, making it easier to organize and compare data during analysis. You can also assign attributes to cases, such as a participant’s age group, gender, occupation, or other characteristics relevant to your research.
Do you need cases? Not always! If each participant has only one interview file, you can assign attributes directly to the file, without creating a separate case for each participant.
Cases become more useful when your data are more complex. For example, you might collect not only multiple interviews with the same participant but also observation notes, field notes, documents, photographs, or other relevant materials. You can use a single case to group all these files and associate them with the same participant attributes. This allows you to examine the participant’s experiences across different data sources, compare what they said in interviews with what you observed or documented, and develop a more comprehensive understanding of their perspectives without treating each file as a separate case.
Cases can also be useful when a single file contains data from multiple participants, as in a focus group transcript. You can create a separate case for each participant and associate relevant segments of the transcript with the appropriate cases. This helps you distinguish participants’ contributions and compare their perspectives, even though their statements appear in the same file. Understanding how they work will be helpful as you begin working with larger or more complex datasets in your own projects.
For this workshop, even though we only have one file per case, we will proceed creating cases, but using a more streamlined approach combining it with attributes.


Attributes
QualCoder also offers the option to Manage Attributes through the Manage menu.
File attributes describe a particular file, whereas case attributes describe the entity represented by the data. For example, an interview’s date and mode of collection are file-level characteristics, while the participant’s age group and occupation are typically case-level characteristics. The choice depends on your research design and what you want to compare during analysis.
File attributes describe individual files. For example, you could record the interview date, interview mode (in-person, telephone, or online), or participant’s age group and occupation for an interview transcript. These attributes are useful when you want to compare files based on their characteristics.
Case attributes describe the people, places, organizations, or situations represented in your data. For example, if you create a case for each participant, you could assign attributes such as age group, occupation, education level, or region. If a participant has several interview files, these attributes belong to the case rather than needing to be repeated for every file. You can then use the attributes to compare participants or explore patterns across groups.






NoteRelevance of Attributes



Attributes will allow you to ask questions like “Do first-year students talk about stress differently from final-year students?”. It allows you to query and explore the data considering demographics and other important characteristics associated with the documents you are analyzing.
Please remember that QualCoder is designed primarily for qualitative data analysis, supporting the systematic coding, organization, comparison, and interpretation of qualitative data. Although attributes can help you describe participants, cases, and other data sources, the main purpose is to support qualitative inquiry rather than statistical analysis. For statistical analysis of attributes, you can export your data to a suitable quantitative analysis tool, such as R.


Attributes can be added manually in the Manage Attributes, Manage Files, Manage Cases or Manage Journals sections by clicking on the (x) button, shown below.

However, there is an easier way to import them from a survey. QualCoder allows researchers to import .csv or .xlsx files with the description of cases and their associated attributes, and we have prepared it for you.
Select Manage Files > Import Survey, then choose the cases-attributes.xlsx file from the workshop folder. This should display as it follows:

Add a mode attribute to indicate whether each interview was conducted online or in person. Set the mode to online for files 01–05 and in-person for files 09–10.

Identify one attribute or combination of attributes that could help uncover a meaningful insight in our data. What would you look for, and why?


If everything looks good, click OK. Now, let’s go to Manage > Cases. Note that the column files shows 0. Why? Because we have yet to link files to cases. Double-click the 0 value to prompt the case file manager window.
Now, we will assign files to cases. Select the corresponding file to match case (participant). We can assign by clicking on the file and choosing “Add selected files to case”.

Before confirming, verify that the name matches the participant listed in the transcript header. Note that the file assignment now displays “YES.” Once you click OK, the grid will update to show 1 file associated with Au Soosaar.
You can also undo assignments or bulk-assign multiple documents within a selected range, though that won’t be relevant in this case. You might also click “Hide Assigned Files” to reduce the list and avoid confusion.

title: Wrap-up
text:
QualCoder is a free, open-source tool for organizing and conducting qualitative data analysis. It lets you bring together text (and other formats such as video and image, not covered in this workshop) in one project, then code your data, write memos, and organize materials into cases and categories. Built-in visualization and reporting features help you spot patterns, compare codes across your data, and share your findings, while support for standard exchange formats keeps your work portable to other qualitative analysis software.
QualCoder can also be integrated with AI tools to support tasks like exploring themes or searching your data. Its design keeps humans in the loop: AI can suggest, but researchers stay at the center of interpretation and decision-making.
This workshop was a quick introduction to the tool. We recognize that every research project is different, and you may run into questions as you apply QualCoder to your own data. The QualCoder documentation and its user community are good places to keep learning.
If you have questions about specific features or about how to set up your project, contact Research Data Services at rds@library.ucsb.edu to schedule a consultation.
